title: GST Council Axes Arrest Powers, Halves Penalties in Sweeping Compliance Overhaul
excerpt: The 57th Council meeting recommended removing GST officers' arrest powers, raising the prosecution threshold to ₹5 crore, and automating refunds and registrations — with no rate changes on the table.
body:
• The 57th GST Council, meeting October 8 in New Delhi under Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, recommended the biggest compliance overhaul since GST's launch: complete removal of tax officers' arrest powers, a prosecution threshold raised from ₹1 crore to ₹5 crore, and the general penalty cut from ₹25,000 to ₹10,000.
  • Refunds get dramatically faster: acknowledgement within 10 days (down from 15), with 90% of eligible claims sanctioned within three working days based on risk assessment; low-risk registrations will be auto-approved within three working days.
  • If you run a business under GST: expect quicker registrations and refunds and no show-cause notices for tax amounts below ₹10,000 — but these are recommendations, not law yet; the process package targets implementation from April 1, 2027, via notifications and rule amendments.
  • Notably absent: any broad rate changes. Rate revisions will now happen only once a year, effective April 1 — the Council's focus has shifted from rates to trust-based, technology-driven administration.

The End of the GST Arrest

The most politically charged recommendation from Thursday's 57th GST Council meeting is also the simplest to state: GST officers will no longer have the power to arrest. The Council recommended omitting Section 69 of the CGST Act entirely, ending an enforcement power that had become a symbol of tax terror for small businesses. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman was careful to add the caveat: "in case of criminality, arrest can be made by enforcement agencies" — the police power disappears from the tax department, not from the state.

Alongside it, the Council raised the criminal prosecution threshold fivefold, from ₹1 crore to ₹5 crore of tax, and removed the minimum-punishment requirement entirely — whether the penalty is a fine, imprisonment, or both will now be left to judicial discretion in every case. The list of offences under Section 132(1) is to be narrowed. For the ordinary late filer, the message is proportionality: recovery, interest, and a proportionate penalty — nothing beyond.

Penalties Cut, Small Notices Killed

The general penalty — the catch-all that applies where no specific penalty is prescribed — drops from ₹25,000 to ₹10,000. Show-cause notices will no longer be issued for tax amounts below ₹10,000. Non-fraud cases get a reduced 5% penalty with no ₹10,000 minimum. The pre-deposit required to appeal a penalty-only order is capped at ₹40 crore, and taxpayers will earn interest on refunded pre-deposits. Before credit can be blocked under Rule 86A, the taxpayer gets a hearing.

Two thorny issues — input tax credit for buyers when the supplier defaults on payment, and ITC on motor vehicles — were referred to a Committee of Officers, a reminder that the compliance war is not fully won.

"The focus is clear: Faster decisions. Lower compliance costs. Automated refunds. Trust-based administration. These are in line with our constant efforts to make GST more efficient, transparent and citizen-friendly."

— Narendra Modi, Prime Minister, on the Council's decisions

Refunds and Registration Go Automatic

The operational centerpiece is speed. Refund acknowledgement falls from 15 days to 10, with deemed acknowledgement if the department misses the window, and 90% of eligible claims are to be sanctioned within three working days based on risk assessment. Registration follows the same logic: low-risk applications get automatic approval within three working days, around two-thirds of amendment applications will be processed automatically, suspended registrations can be restored automatically once the lapse is fixed, and cancellation becomes automatic rather than a months-long ordeal of "running around officials." Taxpayers get a self-correction facility for minor registration errors, and platform warehouses can serve as places of business — a quiet but significant win for e-commerce and small sellers, who can now sell with a place of business in each state.

Input tax credit expands too: GST paid on employee health and life insurance (in eligible cases), telecom towers and pipelines outside factory premises, free samples, and expired stock destroyed as required by law all become creditable. Refunds of input services under the inverted duty structure begin November 1, 2026; plant and machinery follow from April 1, 2027, with the adjustment spread over 60 months.

What It Means and What Comes Next

Taken together, the package moves routine GST administration from the tax officer's desk to the technology platform — the culmination of the "next-generation GST" project that began with last year's landmark rate rationalization. "I don't think there are many outstanding issues which are fundamental to ease of doing business," Sitharaman said. "You can say GST next generation GST, 99 per cent issues have been addressed."

But the fine print matters: Council recommendations do not amend the law by themselves. Every change — from the arrest-power omission to the refund timelines — must travel through statutory amendments to the CGST and IGST Acts, rule changes, notifications, and circulars before taxpayers can rely on it. The process reforms are scheduled from April 1, 2027, and Sitharaman herself said it would take about a year for the new system to fully stabilize. Until the notifications land, the old rules apply — businesses should plan for the new regime, not act on it.
image_caption: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman addresses a media briefing after the 57th GST Council meeting at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, on October 8, 2026. The Council recommended removing GST officers’ arrest powers and halving the general penalty.
nri_angle: For NRIs running India operations or investing in Indian SMEs, the compliance overhaul lowers one of the biggest frictions of doing business in India — arbitrary enforcement risk — which is exactly the kind of structural change that moves the needle on India's ease-of-doing-business story.
author: Diaspora Desk

items.event: Target implementation date for new recommendations.
